reviews.response:
ACCEPTThe additions correctly establish the stated results. I find no required mathematical correction to (3a), (3b), the sharp tree family, the zero-weight counterexample, or the unit-weight  $18\times18$  example. The printed good-route construction is a valid  $162$ -edge perfect matching, and the printed bad-route Hall sets have exactly the asserted  $83/82$  deficiency.I checked the supplied mathematical arguments and coordinate data directly. I have not executed or inspected the checker implementations, and the reported validation counts are not premises of this verdict.1. Positivity characterization (3a)The statement is correct with its two explicit hypotheses: $C_s<\infty$ .Every residual non-direct TH path has strictly positive expense.The first hypothesis matters. It ensures that the equality under consideration is a finite equality; an infeasible instance cannot satisfy the left side merely through an extended-real expression involving infinity.For necessity, let  $N$  be a retaining matching of expense  $b_R+C_s$ . Section 2 supplies at least  $s$  TH terminal components from  $U$  into  $D$ . Choose  $s$  of them, with total expense  $E_{\mathrm{chosen}}$ . Then
$$C_s\le E_{\mathrm{chosen}}
\le f(N)-b_R=C_s.$$
Thus the chosen family is an optimal physical  $C_s$  family, and every other residual TH component has expense zero. The positivity hypothesis makes all those other TH components direct.Restricting  $N$  after deleting the chosen paths and  $R$  therefore gives a perfect matching in the required direct-TH remainder. The paths’ interiors consist of complete actual matched pairs, so this restriction does not leave an actual edge crossing the deletion.This also covers  $s=0$ : the chosen family is empty, and equality forces every residual TH component to be direct.A useful consequence, already implicit in the proof, is:Under the positivity hypothesis, every full matching attaining  $b_R+C_s$  has exactly  $s$  residual non-direct TH components. Those components form a compatible optimal  $C_s$  family.The optimizer supplied by the necessity proof is extracted from an attaining full matching. That is precisely why the conclusion is existential over physical optimizers.The allowance for zero-weight actual edges is also correct. The proof needs positivity of complete non-direct TH paths, not positivity of each individual actual edge. Zero-weight actual edges occurring only in positive-expense TH paths, HH paths, or closed components cause no problem.2. Quantitative route bound (3b)The  $m(N)-s$  accounting is correct. The important point is that every path from  $U$  into  $D$  is non-direct: otherwise its source would belong to
$$F=N_{T'}(D),$$
contrary to membership in  $U=T'\setminus F$ .Consequently, the  $s$  compulsory components selected in the proof are among the  $m(N)$  residual non-direct TH components. This proves  $m(N)\ge s$ . After selecting them, exactly  $m(N)-s$  such components remain.Writing  $\mathcal A$  for the selected family and  $\mathcal B$  for the other non-direct TH components gives
$$f(N)-b_R
=
\sum_{P\in\mathcal A}\operatorname{cost}(P)
+
\sum_{P\in\mathcal B}\operatorname{cost}(P).$$
Direct TH components contribute zero, and HH components and closed components are free. Therefore
$$f(N)-b_R
\ge C_s+(m(N)-s)\eta.$$
Here  $\eta$  must range over all residual non-direct TH paths, with sources in  $T'$  and destinations in  $B'$ . The text uses that global definition correctly. Restricting  $\eta$  to  $U$ -to- $D$  routes would not justify the costs of the remaining components.For  $\eta>0$ , the near-equality conclusion follows exactly:
$$(m(N)-s)\eta\le\epsilon
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m(N)\le s+\left\lfloor\frac{\epsilon}{\eta}\right\rfloor.$$
If  $\eta=0$ , (3b) remains valid but supplies no positive penalty for extra non-direct components. The note appropriately states the floor estimate only for  $\eta>0$ .The no-path caseThe stated no-path clause is correct under its written quantifier: every retaining full matching, if one exists, has  $m(N)=s=0$  and expense  $b_R$ .Indeed,  $m(N)=0$ , while the compulsory-path argument gives  $s\le m(N)$ . All residual TH paths are then direct and free.Absence of a residual non-direct TH path does not itself establish that a retaining completion exists. Without such a completion, one should not infer  $s=0$  solely from the no-path condition. Your wording keeps the conclusion inside the quantification over retaining matchings, and explicitly avoids an expression such as  $0\cdot\infty$ .3. Deleting direct source-terminal arcs measures  $\eta$  exactlyThe proposed one-path test is mathematically correct.In the residual alternating network:A vertex of  $T'$  has no incoming physical arc.A vertex of  $B'$  has no outgoing physical arc.A direct TH path is exactly a single physical arc from  $T'$  to  $B'$ .A non-direct TH path cannot contain a direct  $T'$ -to- $B'$  arc as part of a longer route: such an arc would already connect its initial source to its terminal sink. Therefore deleting all these direct arcs removes precisely the direct TH paths and preserves every non-direct TH path.Conversely, every surviving  $T'$ -to- $B'$  path must enter  $P'$  and use an actual edge, so it is non-direct. Hence
$$\{\text{surviving }T'\text{-to-}B'\text{ paths}\}
=
\{\text{residual non-direct TH paths}\}.$$
A minimum-cost flow of value one in this network therefore has value exactly  $\eta$ , whenever such a path exists. Nonnegative circulations can be removed, so they do not alter that conclusion.The three outcomes have the claimed meanings:One-path outcomeMathematical meaningFinite positive valueEvery residual non-direct TH path has positive expense; the value is  $\eta>0$ .Value zeroA zero-expense non-direct TH path exists.No feasible value-one flowNo residual non-direct TH path exists; the positivity hypothesis holds vacuously.The last outcome is not an infinite lower bound on full-matching expense. The note correctly treats it separately.This test checks the positivity hypothesis. It does not determine whether some optimal  $C_s$  family has a perfect direct remainder, and it does not inspect all such optimizers.4. The connected-tree family is sharpAll parts of this construction check.There are  $4r$  vertices and
$$3r+(r-1)=4r-1$$
edges. The connector edges join the  $r$  four-vertex paths in a chain, so the graph is connected and acyclic.The vertices  $t_i$  and  $z_i$  are leaves. A perfect auxiliary matching must therefore contain
$$t_i b_i,\qquad w_i z_i$$
for every  $i$ . These edges already cover every vertex, proving uniqueness of the full auxiliary matching.For  $D=\{z_1\}$ :There is no direct selected neighbour of  $z_1$ , so  $d=1$ . $W=\varnothing$ , so  $h_D=0$  and  $s=1$ .The path  $t_1,b_1,w_1,z_1$  has expense  $\eta$ .Every non-direct TH path uses at least one actual edge, all of which have weight  $\eta>0$ .Thus the minimum non-direct route expense is indeed the parameter  $\eta$ , and  $C_s=\eta$ .The unique full matching has  $r$  non-direct TH components, each using one actual edge. Consequently,
$$m(N)=r,\qquad f(N)=r\eta
=\eta+(r-1)\eta.$$
This attains (3b). Taking any  $r\ge2$  shows that the coefficient of  $m(N)-s$  cannot be increased in a general bound based on this  $\eta$ .Every selected source  $t_i$  has exactly one  $P$ -neighbour,  $b_i$ . The stated general-graph scope is accurate.5. The zero-weight counterexample worksThe two-row construction has the stated bipartition: for  $r\in\{0,2\}$ , columns  $0,2$  are black and columns  $1,3$  are white. The selected source at column  $3$  enters its row’s actual edge through the black vertex at column  $2$ .For  $D=\{(0,0)\}$ , only the row-0 source can reach  $D$ . Thus
$$d=s=1,\qquad C_s=1,$$
and the unique optimal physical family is the row-0 terminal path.In each component, the leaf vertices force the auxiliary pairs  $0\!-\!1$  and  $2\!-\!3$ . Hence the unique full auxiliary matching has total TH expense
$$1+0=1=C_s.$$
After deleting the row-0 path, the remaining selected source  $(2,3)$  has only the neighbour  $(2,2)\in P$ . The direct-TH restriction deletes that edge, leaving the source unmatched. The direct remainder is therefore infeasible.This establishes exactly the intended failure:
$$f^*=C_s
\quad\text{while no optimal }C_s\text{ family has a perfect direct remainder}.$$
Each selected source has one  $P$ -neighbour. The description as a two-component finite grid-board example, rather than a full rectangle, is correct.The logical conclusion is that the positivity hypothesis cannot be omitted from the general theorem. It does not assert that positivity is necessary for the equivalence to happen to hold in every individual instance; the text makes no such overclaim.6. The unit  $18\times18$  geometry and selection feasibilityThe five footprints are disjoint. Each has thirteen black and twelve white positions; removing its black centre leaves a twelve-edge actual matching. Thus
$$|M|=60,\qquad |P_{\mathrm{black}}|=|P_{\mathrm{white}}|=60.$$
The board has  $162$  vertices of each colour, so  $Q$  has  $102$  of each. Removing the four stated HH sources from the white terminals leaves  $98$  selected sources, consistent with the printed selected list.Every selected white has at most one  $P$ -neighbourThe only exterior white positions adjacent to two different footprints are exactly the four excluded HH sources:White positionIts two  $P$ -neighbours $(5,10)$  $(4,10),(6,10)$  $(6,5)$  $(6,4),(6,6)$  $(10,11)$  $(10,10),(10,12)$  $(11,6)$  $(10,6),(12,6)$ An exterior vertex can have at most one neighbour in any individual square footprint. The remaining pairs of footprints are too far apart to produce another exterior vertex adjacent to both.Thus excluding these four positions leaves every selected white with at most one  $P$ -neighbour. Both proposed TH entrances are selected and have exactly one:
$$(5,8)\sim(6,8),\qquad (8,5)\sim(8,6).$$
This verifies the rectangle’s feasibility claim in addition to the feasibility claims in the tree and zero-weight examples.Both paths are minimum physical solutionsAll five centres have their white neighbours in  $P$ , so  $F=\varnothing$  and  $d=5$ . The four printed HH paths are mutually disjoint and reach the four distinct arm centres, proving  $h_D\ge4$ . There are only four HH sources, so  $h_D=4$  and  $s=1$ .Both
$$A_{\mathrm{bad}}:(5,8),(6,8),(7,8),(8,8)$$
and
$$A_{\mathrm{good}}:(8,5),(8,6),(8,7),(8,8)$$
alternate with the canonical matching and use exactly one actual edge. Every TH route into a centre uses at least one actual edge. Hence both are optimal physical families, with
$$C_1=1.$$
7. The bad route’s forced HH budget and Hall certificates are validThe chamber contains forty vertices: twenty black and twenty white. All are exterior terminals, and none of its white vertices belongs to  $W$ .Its selected neighbourhood is exactly its white set. At the chamber boundary, additional adjacent white vertices are in  $P$  or are the excluded HH sources  $(5,10)$  and  $(6,5)$ . There are no additional selected neighbours outside the chamber.The bad path removes the chamber’s selected white  $(5,8)$ , while removing no chamber black terminal.If every remaining TH path were direct, none could reach any of the other four centres, because those centres have only white  $P$ -neighbours. Thus all four HH sources would have to terminate at the four remaining centres. A terminal component has only one black terminal endpoint, so none of those HH components could also supply a chamber endpoint.All twenty chamber black terminals would consequently need direct selected partners, but only nineteen eligible selected neighbours remain. The contradiction is valid.The printed  $83/82$  witness can be reconstructed exactlyThis larger physical Hall certificate has a simple structural description.After deleting  $A_{\mathrm{bad}}$ , write  $P_B^-$  and  $P_W^-$  for the remaining black and white  $P$ -vertices.
